The maintenance technician was swapping the transfer hose on the parts washer at the quick disconnect fitting. The task was underway because the hose had been reported as weeping at the fitting on the previous shift. Stage of the task: planned maintenance or servicing. Method in effect: WI-905 Parts Washer Hose Replacement. The task was being performed as written. Equipment involved: Parts washer PW-02 transfer line at the quick disconnect fitting. Equipment state at the time: pressurized, hot and energized. Equipment condition: The fitting had been weeping at the seal for about two shifts and was on the maintenance list. PPE in use: Safety glasses, chemical gloves and a face shield, no sleeve protection. This differed from the PPE specified for the task. Immediately before the event: kneeling at the front of the washer with both hands on the quick disconnect and the left forearm resting across the frame about 8 inches below the fitting. At the moment of the event: the disconnect released under residual pressure and heated wash solution sprayed downward across the inner left forearm between the glove cuff and the sleeve. Immediately after the event: the technician pulled back from the machine, called out to Michael at the next bay, and walked to the emergency shower about 20 feet away. The maintenance technician contacted a chemical or harmful substance. Source: Heated caustic wash solution from the parts washer transfer line at the quick disconnect fitting. Magnitude: Approximately 180 degrees Fahrenheit at roughly 4 percent caustic. Contact duration and area: about 2 seconds of spray before the arm was withdrawn, across the inner left forearm. Isolation state: The line was drained at the tank but not depressurized at the fitting, and the written method does not require a pressure check before the disconnect is released. Point of contact and direction of force: across the inner left forearm from the wrist to about 4 inches below the elbow, sprayed from above and to the left. Difference from a normal run of this task: The line normally depressurizes on its own overnight, but this swap was done mid shift with the washer still warm. Conditions at the point of injury: congested or restricted working space and hot. Detail: The space in front of the washer is tight and the technician had to kneel with the forearm resting on the frame to reach the fitting. Timing: About 3 hours into an 8 hour shift and roughly 10 minutes into this task. The maintenance technician had performed this task before. A known hazard, prior near miss, open action or risk assessment covers this task. Detail: The weeping fitting had been reported on the previous shift and a work order was open at the time of the event. A guard, interlock, barrier or control was bypassed, missing, defeated or ineffective. Detail: Sleeve protection is available in the stores but is not listed in the written method for this task, so none was worn. Stop-work opportunity: The swap could have waited until the end of shift when the washer had cooled and the line had depressurized. First aid at the scene: The forearm was irrigated at the emergency shower for about 15 minutes and covered with a sterile dressing. This was given by the site emergency response team. Notification: The supervisor was told within about a minute and EHS attended within five minutes. Scene and equipment: The washer was isolated and locked out and the area was barriered until EHS attended. Work at the location stopped. The maintenance technician was sent to an emergency room for evaluation.
